Lab Atlas · round nine

Marques from circles and ellipses

Five emblems built the way Audi's rings and Toyota's ellipses are: only circles and ellipses, at one consistent weight, symmetrical, with a reason behind every ring. Each one is shown flat, stamped in chrome, and as its construction drawing.

Only primitives

Every line is an arc of a circle or an ellipse, with nothing freehand. That gives these marks the machined calm of a car badge.

One weight

A single stroke weight per mark, or Toyota-style rings whose weight comes from offsetting two ellipses.

Symmetry and linkage

Rings overlap, interlock or share a centre, like Audi's four and Toyota's three.

A reason for each ring

Meridians, the equator, the titan's arch, an orbit, an armillary sphere, three linked kinds of lab. Each part stands for something.

01

Horizon

A wide ellipse holds an A made of two circular arcs. The A's apex touches the top of the rim and its feet stand on the bottom. The equator runs straight across, rim to rim, and serves as the crossbar. The mark reads as two meridians meeting at the pole, or as an A standing on the horizon.

02

Atlas Arch

Atlas reduced to geometry. A pointed arch of two circular arcs forms the A, and it carries a globe on its apex the way the titan carries the heavens. The globe is a circle with one meridian and one parallel, and a straight crossbar completes the letter.

03

Orbit A

A pointed A of two circular arcs, with a tilted elliptical orbit woven through its legs: over the left leg, under the right. The orbit is the crossbar, and it turns the letter into a small world with something circling it.

04

Armillary

A circle and two tilted ellipses woven over and under one another, like the rings of an armillary sphere, the old instrument for modelling the heavens. Audi's rings link side by side; these link around one centre, so the mark reads as a globe.

05

Borromean

Three rings in a triangle, linked so that no two are joined but all three hold together: cut any one and the others fall apart. The top ring and the two lower ones sit where an A's apex and feet would be. For Lab Atlas they stand for the wet lab, the computer and the field, which only work together.
